name: French Third Republic
info: The parliamentary republic that governed France from 1870 to 1940, the longest-lasting French system of government since 1789, which built a vast colonial empire and won the First World War.

facts.capital: Paris (the government sat at Tours in 1870 and at Versailles in 1871)
facts.founder: Parisian deputies led by Léon Gambetta (Government of National Defence)
facts.successor: Vichy France (the French State) and Free France

t: The Third Republic was proclaimed on 4 September 1870, after Napoleon III's capture at the Battle of Sedan, and lasted until 10 July 1940.
Intended as a provisional government while monarchists disagreed over a king, it became France's permanent form of government under the constitutional laws of 1875.
It built a colonial empire second in size only to the British Empire, extending over 13,500,000 km2 at its height in the 1920s and 1930s.
dyk: To discourage the monarchists, the French Crown Jewels were broken up and sold in 1885; only a few crowns were kept, their precious gems replaced by coloured glass.
ev: Parisian deputies led by Léon Gambetta establish the Government of National Defence
The Treaty of Frankfurt ends the Franco-Prussian War, and the Paris Commune is bloodily suppressed
Parliamentary acts establish the constitutional laws of the republic
The Jules Ferry laws make public education free, mandatory and secular
The Dreyfus affair divides France until Alfred Dreyfus is exonerated
The law on the separation of Church and State abolishes Napoleon's Concordat of 1801
France fights the First World War and emerges on the winning side
After the Fall of France, parliament gives full powers to Marshal Philippe Pétain

sections.foundation:
The Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 brought down Napoleon III and his Second French Empire. After his capture at the Battle of Sedan on 1 September 1870, Parisian deputies led by Léon Gambetta set up the Government of National Defence on 4 September, with General Louis-Jules Trochu as its president. It ruled through the Siege of Paris, and Gambetta left the city in a hot air balloon to establish the government at Tours. After the surrender of January 1871, a conservative National Assembly made Adolphe Thiers head of the executive and signed the Treaty of Frankfurt on 10 May 1871, ceding Alsace and most of Lorraine to the new German Empire.

In Paris, workers and National Guards rose and took power as the Paris Commune, which the army under Patrice de MacMahon crushed in the Bloody Week of May 1871. The monarchist majority agreed on the Comte de Chambord as king, but he would not accept the tricolour flag, so a "temporary" republic was set up. The constitutional laws of February 1875 created a president, a Chamber of Deputies and a Senate. After MacMahon's crisis of 16 May 1877, republicans won both houses, and in 1879 he resigned, ending the prospect of a restoration.
sections.socioeconomy:
France was a rural nation, and the peasant farmer was the typical citizen. Eugen Weber argued in Peasants into Frenchmen that railroads, republican schools and conscription gave rural France a sense of national identity by about 1900, though some scholars hold it existed before 1870. Paris led a new consumer culture: department stores such as Le Bon Marché and La Samaritaine sold at fixed prices, and Émile Zola set Au Bonheur des Dames in one. The daily press of Paris grew from 1 million copies in 1870 to 5 million in 1910, though banks and foreign governments secretly paid papers for favourable coverage.

The welfare state lagged behind Germany and Britain: an accident insurance law came in 1898 and a voluntary national pension plan in 1910. The First World War caused damage of about 113% of the GDP of 1913, and the national debt rose from 66% of GDP to 170% in 1919. The economy prospered from 1926 to 1929 after Raymond Poincaré balanced the budget. The Great Depression came late, around 1931, and was relatively mild. In 1936 the Popular Front brought a 40-hour week and two weeks of paid holiday.
sections.military:
After 1871 France rebuilt its army, with new artillery and, after 1905, heavy investment in military aircraft. Its colonial armies fought the Sino-French War of 1884–1885, in which Admiral Courbet destroyed the Chinese fleet at Fuzhou, and suppressed rebellions in Morocco in 1925, Syria in 1926 and Indochina in 1930. In 1913 military service was extended from two years to three.

In the First World War the Anglo-French victory at the Battle of the Marne in September 1914 defeated Germany's plan for a quick win, and the war became one of trench warfare and attrition, reaching its height at Verdun and the Somme; 1.5 million French soldiers died. By 1918 France produced more munitions and artillery than its allies. Between the wars it built the Maginot Line along the German border. In 1939 the commander in chief, Maurice Gamelin, saw little action in the Phoney War beyond the Saar Offensive. In May 1940 he sent his best divisions north under the Dyle Plan, while German forces crossed the Ardennes and the River Meuse near Sedan. The historian Julian Jackson holds that the plan was destined for failure.
sections.governance:
The republic had a president as head of state, a directly elected Chamber of Deputies and an indirectly elected Senate, with a ministry under the President of the Council. When Jules Grévy succeeded MacMahon in 1879 he promised not to use the power of dissolution, which made the system parliamentary until 1940. Governing coalitions rarely lasted more than a few months; the journalist John Gunther counted 103 cabinets with an average length of eight months.

Politics were sharply polarized between a reformist France heir to the Revolution and a conservative France rooted in the peasantry, the Church and the army. Republicans weakened the Catholic Church: the Ferry laws of 1881 and 1882 made schools secular, Émile Combes closed parochial schools and banned the religious orders, and the law of 1905 separated Church and State. The Radical Party, founded in 1901, was the most important party of the early 20th century, and the Democratic Republican Alliance became the main centre-right party. The republic survived the Boulanger crisis of 1889, the Panama scandals of 1892, the Dreyfus affair and the riot of 6 February 1934, when police killed 15 demonstrators.
sections.impact:
Under the expansionist Jules Ferry the republic acquired Indochina, Madagascar, vast territories in West and Central Africa and much of Polynesia. The colonies were ruled under the claim of a civilizing mission, and Catholic missionaries worked to convert their peoples. By 1939 a third of French exports went to the colonies; settlers' land in Algeria grew from 1,600,000 hectares in 1890 to 2,700,000 in 1940. After the First World War, France regained Alsace–Lorraine, occupied the Saar Basin, shared Germany's African colonies such as Kamerun with Britain and took the Mandate of Syria and the Mandate of Lebanon.

In Europe its diplomacy moved from isolation in 1871 to the centre of the alliance system in 1914, through the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894 and the Entente Cordiale of 1904 with Britain. The Dreyfus affair, in which Émile Zola's J'accuse exposed the army's case against a Jewish officer, became a universal symbol of injustice. The republic was the first stable republican government in French history and the first to win majority support, and the Fourth Republic that followed was a parliamentary system not unlike it.
sections.decline:
The interwar years were marked by strife between right and left. France sought allies against Germany but found the United States and Britain unwilling to commit and its Eastern European allies weak. When Germany remilitarized the Rhineland on 7 March 1936, nothing was done, and in 1938 Édouard Daladier signed the Munich Agreement, which gave the Sudetenland to Nazi Germany. Rearmament, begun in 1936, bore fruit only in 1939 and 1940.

After Germany invaded Poland, Britain and France declared war in 1939. Paul Reynaud replaced Daladier in March 1940, and after the German breakthrough of May and June he refused to support an armistice and resigned on 16 June. On 10 July 1940 the French parliament gave full powers to Marshal Philippe Pétain, who proclaimed the French State at Vichy, while Charles de Gaulle called on the French to rally to Free France. Vichy never formally abolished the republic, which, in Jackson's words, "surreptitiously disappeared". Historians have long debated whether the collapse reflected a national "decadence", as Marc Bloch and Jean-Baptiste Duroselle argued, or military and structural causes, as Robert J. Young and those who followed him argued.

summary: The French Third Republic was born of defeat in 1870 and meant to be temporary, yet it became the longest-lasting French regime since 1789. It secularized schools and separated Church and State, built the second largest colonial empire and won the First World War, but its unstable coalitions could not meet Nazi Germany, and it ended with the Fall of France in 1940.
references: Philippe Bernard, The Decline of the Third Republic, 1914–1938 (Cambridge University Press, 1985)
Eugen Weber, The Hollow Years: France in the 1930s (Norton, 1994)
Robert Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (Macmillan, 1996)
Robert J. Young, An Uncertain Idea of France (P. Lang, 2005)

pointDescs.1870: After Napoleon III's capture at Sedan, the Government of National Defence is proclaimed on 4 September and Paris is besieged.
pointDescs.1871: France surrenders, signs the Treaty of Frankfurt and loses Alsace and most of Lorraine; the Paris Commune is suppressed.
pointDescs.1875: The constitutional laws establish a president, a Chamber of Deputies and a Senate.
pointDescs.1879: Republicans win the Senate, MacMahon resigns, and Jules Grévy's presidency makes the system parliamentary.
pointDescs.1885: Under Jules Ferry the colonial empire expands after the Sino-French War of 1884–1885, and the Crown Jewels are sold.
pointDescs.1894: The Franco-Russian Alliance is formed and the Dreyfus affair begins.
pointDescs.1904: The Entente Cordiale ends a long period of Anglo-French hostility.
pointDescs.1914: France enters the First World War, and the Battle of the Marne saves Paris.
pointDescs.1919: The Treaty of Versailles returns Alsace–Lorraine and brings mandates over Syria and Lebanon.
pointDescs.1926: Poincaré balances the budget and stabilizes the franc; the economy prospers until 1929.
pointDescs.1931: The Great Depression reaches France, later and milder than elsewhere.
pointDescs.1936: The Popular Front takes power, and Germany remilitarizes the Rhineland unopposed.
pointDescs.1938: Daladier signs the Munich Agreement, sacrificing the alliance with Czechoslovakia.
pointDescs.1940: Germany defeats France, and on 10 July parliament gives full powers to Pétain.

notes: The article's reference lists are empty in the saved text, so references are [].
The capital is not stated as such; Paris, Tours (1870) and Versailles (1871) are named as seats in the article.
Point strengths are my judgement; the peak at 1919 reflects victory and the colonial empire's height in the 1920s.
